scope: Any equality test on the diagnosis field.
description: The diagnosis field is a free-text list, not an atomic category. Many patients carry several comma-separated diseases in one value, so testing exact equality against a single disease name silently drops every patient whose disease is co-listed with others. Disease membership must be tested as containment of the disease designation within the field.

scope: Any comparison of disease designations across the patient and examination tables.
description: The two tables carrying a diagnosis use different spellings for the same diseases. The patient table writes the Sjogren and Behcet designators in upper case, while the examination table writes them in mixed case, and lupus is written identically in both. Matching a disease name across the two tables therefore has to be case-insensitive, and a case-sensitive comparison against one table's spelling will miss matches in the other.

scope: Patients whose diagnosis designator carries a suspicion suffix.
description: Several diagnosis values carry a trailing suspicion marker appended to the disease designator, meaning the disease was suspected rather than confirmed. Such values still contain the disease designation, so a containment test treats suspected cases as diagnosed ones; if only confirmed diagnoses are wanted, the suspicion marker has to be excluded explicitly.

scope: Disease counts computed from the examination table.
description: More than a third of examination records carry no diagnosis at all, and a small number carry no examination date. Disease frequency computed from the examination table therefore reflects only the covered examinations, whereas the patient table carries a diagnosis for every patient row.

scope: Any analysis that combines an examination-based finding with patient demographics.
description: The examination table and the patient table do not share a substantial identifier population: only a small minority of examination identifiers also exist as patient identifiers, and most identifiers are entirely absent from the patient table. Combining an examination finding such as a coagulation result with patient attributes such as sex or birthday therefore discards most examination rows and cannot be assumed to be a full join. The examination table also contains rows with no identifier at all.

scope: Patient counts and per-patient aggregates over laboratory data.
description: The laboratory table is one row per patient per test date, and one patient can contribute many rows. Counting rows therefore counts measurements rather than patients, and a patient-level result requires de-duplication of identifiers. Cohort questions that overlap several analytes on the same row also have to decide whether they require the analytes to co-occur on one row or merely to occur for the same patient at some time.

scope: Laboratory-based cohorts.
description: Every laboratory identifier resolves to a patient record, but laboratory data covers only a minority of the patient cohort, so laboratory-defined cohorts are a subset of the patient table rather than a full-cohort view.

scope: Any split of patients by admission type.
description: Admission type is encoded as a sign: a plus sign marks in-patients and a minus sign marks out-patients. Two qualifications apply. First, a small number of rows carry a malformed variant of the plus code, which would be excluded by an exact match on the plus sign. Second, a number of rows carry no admission code at all, so a strict two-way comparison of in-patients and out-patients does not sum to the whole cohort.

scope: Sex filters over the patient cohort.
description: Sex is recorded as a single upper-case letter, one letter for male and one for female. A small number of patient rows have no sex recorded, so male and female counts do not add up to the full patient count.

scope: Age filters and average-age aggregation.
description: Age is not stored; it is derived per patient as the difference between the year of the reference date and the year of birth, which ignores the month and day. A birth-year window is therefore the year part of the birthday. One patient row has no birthday and one carries a birthday far outside the cohort's era, so both affect an unrestricted age average.

scope: Questions about whether a patient's record data was recorded.
description: The field used to decide whether a patient's data was recorded is a date field, not a flag. A populated value means the patient's descriptive record carries a date; an absent value is what the workload treats as data not recorded. The field should therefore be tested for presence rather than compared with any particular date value. For a subset of patients the recorded description date predates the patient's first recorded date, so the two date fields are not ordered consistently.

scope: Interpreting a normal or negative autoantibody finding in the laboratory table.
description: A normal autoantibody finding is not expressed as a numeric zero. Across the autoantibody columns the negative result is written as a word meaning negative and, for several columns, also as a zero-valued code; these two encodings coexist in the same column for the same marker and both mean negative. A further consequence is that a test for normality that lists only the single-letter negative code and the plus-minus code matches nothing in this data for anti-centromere, anti-scl70 and anti-SSB, because those encodings do not occur in those columns. Since most laboratory rows leave the autoantibody columns empty, normality also has to be distinguished from a missing measurement.

scope: Reading the three coagulation assays.
description: Each of the three assays is a positive/negative code: a plus sign marks a positive result and a minus sign marks a negative one. The three assays are far from fully populated, and a blank assay is not a negative result: it means that assay was not recorded for that examination. Treating blanks as negatives changes the size of every coagulation cohort.

trigger_keywords: positive measure of degree of coagulation
scope: Defining a positive coagulation cohort.
description: A positive degree of coagulation holds when any one of the three assays is positive; the status is a disjunction across the panel, not a requirement that all three agree. A strict conjunction yields a much smaller cohort than the disjunction and is not the intended reading of a positive measure.

scope: Thrombosis-level cohort selection.
description: The degree of thrombosis is a small ordinal scale with four levels, from no thrombotic involvement through three increasing grades. A specified thrombosis level is an equality test on the grade; level zero means absence of thrombosis and must not be conflated with a missing value, since zero is recorded explicitly for most examinations.

scope: Filtering patients who did or did not have recorded symptoms.
description: Recorded symptoms are present on exactly those examinations whose thrombosis grade is above zero, and absent on every examination with grade zero. Having symptoms is therefore equivalent to a non-zero thrombosis grade, and having no recorded symptom is equivalent to grade zero; the equivalence is exact in the observed data. Because the field lives on the examination table, a symptom-based cohort is also subject to the sparse linkage between examinations and patient records.

scope: Any question that mentions ANA or an ANA pattern.
description: The examination record carries two distinct antinuclear antibody fields: a numeric titre and a text pattern. The single-letter pattern designators such as the one meaning speckled belong to the text pattern field, which is the field that answers a question about a pattern consisting of only one code; the numeric titre field holds dilution values and never holds letters. Referring a letter pattern to the numeric field returns nothing.

scope: Matching a specific ANA pattern value.
description: Pattern values are inconsistent in case and in the separator used between co-occurring pattern codes: the same letter appears in both upper and lower case, some combinations are separated by a comma and others by a period, and the order of the codes within a combination is not fixed. A pattern consisting of only one code is stored as that single letter with no separator. Case-sensitive or order-sensitive matching, or a containment match that ignores separators, gives different cohorts, and the varying encodings have to be normalised before comparison. The field is also blank for many examinations where the titre is populated, so pattern and titre are not recorded together consistently.

scope: Classifying an albumin measurement as low.
description: Blood albumin values below four are treated as low for this workload; the qualifying condition is a strict lower bound on the analyte. The average of the analyte is taken over individual laboratory rows rather than over patients.

scope: Elevated platelet count filtering.
description: A platelet count above four hundred is treated as elevated for this workload. The platelet count is measured many times per patient, so a cohort defined by an elevated platelet count spans many laboratory rows and requires de-duplication when patients are counted.

scope: Classifying GPT as elevated, including per-patient history flags.
description: Two thresholds are used for GPT in this workload: a value above thirty is the threshold used when a question names that cut-off explicitly, while a value at or above sixty is what counts as exceeding the reference interval for the enzyme. The two are not interchangeable. A patient-level history flag for elevated GPT is formed by asking whether any of that patient's laboratory rows crosses the applicable threshold, which is an existential test over the patient's rows rather than a filter on a single row.

scope: Classifying blood glucose as outside the normal range.
description: Blood glucose at or above one hundred and eighty is the condition used for a glucose value that is not within the normal range in this workload. This is a one-sided rule: the upper deviation is what the workload tests, so a low glucose value is not captured by it.

scope: Classifying total cholesterol as normal or high.
description: Total cholesterol below two hundred and fifty is within the normal range, and a value at or above two hundred and fifty is the condition for high cholesterol in this workload. The two readings are complements of one another, and a normal-cholesterol cohort therefore excludes every row at or above the cut-off while also excluding rows with no measurement.

scope: Classifying creatinine phosphokinase as normal or elevated.
description: A creatinine phosphokinase value below two hundred and fifty is within the normal range for this workload, and a value at or above two hundred and fifty is beyond the normal range. Note that the enzyme can legitimately be measured as zero, so a normal-range cohort that only tests the upper bound also contains zero-valued rows rather than treating zero as missing.

scope: Classifying creatinine as abnormal.
description: A creatinine value at or above one and a half is the condition for an abnormal creatinine level in this workload. This is a one-sided upper rule.

scope: Identifying a borderline-passing urea nitrogen value.
description: The workload treats a urea nitrogen value of exactly twenty-nine as sitting just within the borderline of passing. Because the analyte is integer-valued, the qualifying condition is an equality on that single integer, not a range.

scope: Defining a normal immunoglobulin G cohort.
description: A normal immunoglobulin G level is a value strictly above nine hundred and strictly below two thousand, an interval bounded on both sides. Both bounds are exclusive, so values equal to either bound fall outside the normal cohort.

scope: Defining an abnormal immunoglobulin M cohort.
description: An immunoglobulin M level at or below forty, or at or above four hundred, is abnormal for this workload; the normal band lies strictly between the two bounds. The rule is a disjunction of a low deviation and a high deviation, so both tails must be included; the low tail also captures zero-valued immunoglobulin measurements.

scope: Averages and relative comparisons computed over the anti-cardiolipin IgM level.
description: The anti-cardiolipin IgM level contains one value several orders of magnitude above every other observation, while the remaining values stay in the low hundreds; the column mean is therefore pulled far above the typical level. Any comparison against the column average, including a percentage-above-average test, is dominated by that single record and should be read with that in mind.

scope: Classifying C-reactive protein as abnormal.
description: C-reactive protein is recorded as a semi-quantitative text code rather than as a number. An abnormal, raised result is expressed by a plus-style code, and results range from negative codes through single and multiple plus codes to numeric-looking strings including less-than codes. A comparison that expects a numeric threshold will not classify these values, and detecting an abnormal result means detecting a positive plus-style code.

scope: Immunoglobulin G cohort definition.
description: Immunoglobulin G is unmeasured on the large majority of laboratory rows, far more often than the other analytes in the panel. A cohort defined by a normal immunoglobulin G level is therefore drawn from a small subset of the laboratory data even though the panel as a whole is large.

scope: Date-window filtering of laboratory data.
description: The laboratory test dates span roughly two decades, from the early eighties to the late nineties, and every laboratory row carries a valid date within that span. The examination dates occupy a shorter window, and the workload's date windows fall inside the laboratory span, so a phrase about being examined within a date range is applied to the laboratory test date when the cohort is defined by laboratory values. The window comparison is inclusive at both ends.
